children: By Corrie Driebusch and Benoît Morenne
Texas Stock Exchange's audacious plan to challenge Wall Street's financial dominance hinges on convincing companies to ditch their New York listings.
Pipeline company Energy Transfer is set to be the first major company to switch its primary listing from New York to TXSE, according to people familiar with the matter.
The $75 billion company plans to move its listing from the New York Stock Exchange as soon as next month, the people said.
TXSE, pronounced "tex-ee," launched in 2024. Its founder James Lee aimed to capitalize on state politicians' efforts to elevate Texas in the business world.

Energy Transfer's executive chairman Kelcy Warren, who Forbes estimates is worth over $9 billion, is a major backer of TXSE's parent company. He owns a roughly 30% stake in TXSE Group, according to a 2025 filing, and was one of its earliest investors, along with BlackRock and Citadel Securities.

TXSE began offering trading in U.S.-listed stocks in July. But it hasn't yet had primary listings, meaning it misses out on the opening and closing auction trades, which are typically the most active and therefore lucrative for exchanges. Companies also pay exchanges annual listing fees that can climb into the hundreds of thousands of dollars.
TXSE has attracted multiple exchange-traded funds to list on it in the coming weeks, but Energy Transfer, which is based in Dallas, would be the first big corporate listing.

More companies are expected to announce plans to switch to TXSE in the coming weeks, according to people familiar with the matter. Still, other upstart exchanges have struggled to gain traction and it is far from guaranteed TXSE will become a dominant player.

The NYSE and its midtown rival the Nasdaq have long battled to win stock listings, showering companies with lavish parties, big marketing budgets and other perks. Convincing a company to switch its listing exchange is viewed as a major coup. Last year Walmart switched its listing from NYSE, where it had traded for more than 50 years, to the Nasdaq.

While the Nasdaq and the NYSE have long held a virtual duopoly on stock listings, there are many stock-trading venues, and trading is fragmented. The current daily trading volume for TXSE is less than 1% of the total U.S. equity volume, according to Cboe Global Markets data.

As part of its effort to attract more business, Texas also established its own business courts to take on Delaware's stronghold as the country's corporate capital, moves that have been applauded by executives including Energy Transfer's Warren and Elon Musk.
"With Texas there's no surprises. You understand the laws, and they understand you, and you go about your job," Warren said at a Dallas conference in late 2024.
